# Hollywood, Media, and California's Parallel Platform {#sec-4-08}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act III — The Silicon Valley Machine · 1908–1990
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** Why did the film industry go west?

**The answer.** To escape patent enforcement. Edison's trust controlled film
equipment patents and enforced them aggressively on the east coast, so
filmmakers went to southern California — far from process servers, close to a
foreign border, and blessed with light. California's second great industry was
founded by people fleeing a monopoly, and it promptly built one of its own.

**The mechanism.** Chokepoint control, in a second medium, with an instructive
difference: Hollywood's bottleneck is distribution and its product is narrative.
Together with the Valley it constitutes California's dual power — whoever
controls the code and whoever controls the story.

**The key fact.** The studio system was broken by an antitrust decree in 1948
that forced the studios to divest their theatre chains. The lesson California's
elite took from it was not to stop integrating vertically but to stop owning the
physical layer where the courts can see it.

**The human anchor.** A filmmaker in 1910 heading west specifically to be beyond
the reach of a patent lawyer, and finding a place that will let him build a
bigger version of the thing he is escaping.

**Excluded voices.** Everyone the studio system's contracts bound and its
casting practices excluded; the blacklist; and the workers whose 1945 and 1946
strikes are absent from every romantic account of the period.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that the same chokepoint logic operated in
California's cultural industry by showing an industry founded to escape a patent
monopoly reconstitute one around distribution within fifteen years.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

Filmmakers went to southern California to get away from a lawyer. Thomas
Edison's Motion Picture Patents Company controlled the equipment patents and
enforced them aggressively on the east coast, and distance from process servers
— with a foreign border nearby if the distance proved insufficient — was the
only reliable defence. The light and the varied landscape were real advantages
and they were not the reason.

California's second great industry was therefore founded by people fleeing a
monopoly, and it built a larger one within fifteen years. The studios integrated
vertically across production, distribution, and exhibition, and the chokepoint
they held was distribution: whoever controls the screens determines what gets
made. The star system turned performers into contracted assets whose
desirability was manufactured and whose careers were owned, which is a
credential of a different kind.

In 1948 the antitrust consent decrees forced the studios to divest their theatre
chains, and the chapter is precise about what that broke. It broke ownership of
the physical layer, which was the visible part. The lesson California's elite
drew was not to stop integrating but to stop owning the layer a court can point
at — and the chapter points forward to platforms that will control logistics,
moderation, and terms of service while insisting they are not publishers.

Together with the Valley this constitutes California's dual power. One industry
controls the code and the other controls the story, and both are chokepoints on
something that used to be free.

The costs are well documented and rarely included in the romance: the contract
system that bound workers to studios, the casting practices that excluded most
of the country from appearing in its own films, the strikes of 1945 and 1946
that were broken with force, and the blacklist that followed.

Two industries, one state, one logic. By the end of this chapter the reader
should expect the pattern anywhere California builds anything.
:::

::: {.chapter-question}
Why did the film industry go west?
:::

The film industry went west to get away from a lawyer.

Thomas Edison held the core patents on motion picture equipment, and in 1908 he
consolidated them with the other significant holders into the Motion Picture
Patents Company — a trust that licensed cameras, projectors, and film stock, set
the terms of the business, and enforced its position aggressively through
litigation and, by numerous accounts, through methods that did not involve
courts.

Independent producers who would not take a licence needed distance. Southern
California offered it: three thousand miles from the trust's enforcement
apparatus, and close enough to the Mexican border that a production could cross
it if a process server arrived.

The light was genuinely good and the landscape genuinely varied, and both
feature in every account. They are not why the industry moved. It moved to
escape a monopoly, and within fifteen years it had built a larger one.

## The trust broken, the structure rebuilt

The Patents Company was dissolved by antitrust action in the mid-1910s, having
already been overtaken commercially by the independents it had tried to
suppress.

What replaced it was the studio system, and it was integrated more completely
than the trust had ever managed. The major studios owned production — the lots,
the equipment, the crews. They owned distribution. And critically they owned
exhibition: chains of theatres, including the first-run houses in major cities
where a film made most of its money.

That last link is the chokepoint. A film that cannot get into theatres does not
exist commercially, and the studios owned the theatres. The practice of block
booking required an exhibitor who wanted a studio's desirable pictures to take
its undesirable ones as a package, which meant independent producers could not
get screens even in theatres the studios did not own.

The mechanism is identical to the Southern Pacific deciding which Central Valley
towns would exist. Control the passage and you control everything that must
pass.

## Contracts

The other asset was people, held under long-term contracts of a kind that would
now be unlawful.

A studio contract player was paid a salary, assigned to pictures, loaned to
other studios at a profit, and suspended without pay for refusing a role — with
the suspension period added to the end of the contract, so that refusal extended
the term indefinitely. Names were changed, biographies invented, appearances
managed, and personal conduct governed by morals clauses.

Olivia de Havilland sued Warner Bros. over the suspension practice and won in
1944, in a California decision that limited personal service contracts to seven
calendar years and is still known in the industry by her name. It was one of the
few successful challenges to the system from inside it.

The parallel to a credential is exact enough to be worth stating. A studio, like
a university, took raw material, certified it, and controlled the terms on which
it reached the market. Stardom was manufactured, and the manufacturer kept the
plant.

## 1948

The system was broken by *United States v. Paramount Pictures*, decided in 1948,
which held the studios' practices unlawful and led to consent decrees requiring
them to divest their theatre chains.

The chapter should be precise about what that broke. It broke ownership of the
physical distribution layer — the buildings with seats in them, which anyone
could see and a court could point at. It did not break the studios' control of
finance, of distribution relationships, or of the talent pipeline, and the
industry reorganised around those within a decade.

The lesson California's cultural industry took is the same lesson its railroad
had taught in Act I chapter 10: do not own the visible physical layer, because
that is the layer a court can reach.

Hold that against Act IV, where a company will argue at length that it is not a
publisher and therefore not responsible for what it distributes, while operating
the largest distribution system in human history. The studios owned theatres and
were forced to sell them. The platforms own no theatres, and there is nothing to
divest.

## Water, and the other thing Los Angeles took

The film industry could not have grown where it did without a supply of water
that southern California does not have, and the acquisition of that water is the
same story as everything else in this act.

The Los Angeles Aqueduct, completed in 1913, brought water two hundred and
thirty miles from the Owens Valley on the eastern side of the Sierra. The city's
agents had bought land and water rights in the valley, in some cases without
disclosing who they represented or what the purpose was, and the diversion
progressively destroyed the valley's agriculture. Owens Lake dried to a salt
flat that has been a source of dust pollution ever since. Valley residents
dynamited sections of the aqueduct in the 1920s and lost.

Public infrastructure, built with municipal bonds, delivered water whose first
and largest beneficiaries included landowners in the San Fernando Valley who had
bought property in advance of the route being announced, and who then had it
annexed to the city so it could be irrigated.

This is Act I chapter 9 with a pipe instead of a rail line: public money, a
route determined by people with prior positions along it, and a resource
transferred from a place with no political weight to a place with all of it.

Los Angeles then grew from a modest city to the second largest in the country,
and the industry that had come west to escape a patent lawyer grew with it.

## Dual power

California ended up with two industries built on the same logic in different
media, four hundred miles apart, and the pairing is the chapter's argument.

The Valley controls the code: the operating systems, the networks, the search
index, the models. Hollywood controls the story: the narrative forms and the
distribution of attention that shape what a culture believes about itself.

Both are chokepoints on something that used to be free. Anyone could tell a
story before there was a studio system, and anyone could compute before there
was a platform. Both industries interposed themselves between a capability and
its audience, and both became extremely profitable by charging for the passage.

They also converged. Media and technology companies have been buying each other
since the 1980s, streaming has moved distribution wholly onto the Valley's
infrastructure, and the largest film financier and the largest search company
now run on the same kind of recommendation system. By the 2010s the distinction
was substantially a matter of headquarters.

## Who paid

The costs of the studio system are documented in the industry's own records.

Contract labour below the line — crews, technicians, extras — worked hours that
produced the strikes of 1945 and 1946, which were broken with force and with the
cooperation of rival unions. Casting practice excluded most of the American
population from appearing in its own national cinema except in stereotyped
roles, under a production code that among other things prohibited depicting
relationships across racial lines. And from 1947 the blacklist removed hundreds
of writers, directors, and performers from employment on political grounds,
enforced not by statute but by studios acting in concert with each other.

That last point is worth registering. The blacklist was a private arrangement
among companies, administered through informal clearance procedures, with no
legal authority and no appeal. It is the Committee of Vigilance from Act I
chapter 7 in a different industry: private actors performing a governmental
function, competently and with the approval of respectable opinion, because the
formal apparatus was too slow.

Two industries, one state, one logic. By the end of this chapter the reader
should expect the pattern anywhere California builds anything.
